title: Generative AI for Patient-Centric Healthcare
summary: A 150-minute masterclass for doctors, hospital leaders, pharma professionals, educators and researchers, built around clinician-in-the-loop practice and synthetic data.
notes: Open by asking participants to name one task that consumes time but does not require autonomous clinical judgement. Reinforce that the programme is 60 minutes of theory followed by 90 minutes of hands-on work.
cue: Ask: Where could GenAI create patient value without taking decision authority away from a professional?

title: Why GenAI Matters in Healthcare and Pharma
summary: The slide contrasts the scale of information and documentation burden with what GenAI can support and what it must never do autonomously.
notes: Use the three-column logic: challenge, capability, limitation. Ask participants to distinguish drafting support from diagnosis or treatment authority.
cue: Run a quick poll: Which is the bigger problem in your setting—documentation, evidence search, patient communication or data analysis?

title: Twelve Application Categories
summary: A functional map of GenAI tools across patient communication, multilingual education, documentation, reasoning, research, medical affairs, pharmacovigilance, trials, analytics, design, operations and governance.
notes: Do not teach tools as a popularity list. Teach selection by task, data sensitivity, patient impact, evidence requirements, and the institution-approved environment.
cue: Choose one category and ask: what evidence or data would this tool need, and who must approve the output?

title: Patient-Centric Applications
summary: GenAI can help simplify discharge instructions, prepare multilingual counselling, support shared decision-making aids and visualize patient journeys.
notes: Emphasize health literacy, teach-back, cultural context and the risk of altering medicine names, doses or clinical probabilities during simplification or translation.
cue: Ask participants to recall a discharge or counselling failure caused by misunderstanding rather than lack of clinical knowledge.

title: Doctor Productivity: Documentation and Reasoning
summary: High-value workflows include OPD summaries, SOAP notes, referral letters, prior-authorisation drafts, differential diagnosis checklists, red-flag extraction and follow-up plans.
notes: Separate documentation assistance from clinical reasoning. Use de-identified or synthetic cases in general-purpose tools and require explicit review before any content enters a clinical record.
cue: Demonstrate how a chain-of-verification prompt forces supporting, opposing and missing evidence to remain visible.

title: Medical Affairs, Safety and Clinical Trials
summary: GenAI can support balanced medical-information drafts, adverse-event intake, KOL briefings, trial eligibility summaries, regulatory-safe internal communication and literature surveillance.
notes: All external pharma outputs remain subject to medical, legal and regulatory review. Avoid promotional drift, unsupported causality, and hidden changes to protocol or label language.
cue: Ask: Which parts of a medical-information response can be drafted by AI, and which parts require accountable professional sign-off?

title: Literature Review to Manuscript
summary: The research workflow moves from PICO and source discovery to evidence tables, gap extraction, drafting support, reference management and disclosure of AI assistance.
notes: Keep search strategies reproducible, verify every citation against the source, distinguish extracted facts from inference and disclose material AI assistance according to journal policy.
cue: Compare semantic discovery tools with PubMed: exploration can be AI-assisted, but systematic coverage needs an explicit reproducible method.

title: Safety, Privacy, Ethics and Governance
summary: The slide links regulatory principles with four recurring risks: hallucination, bias, privacy breach and over-reliance, followed by debate cases.
notes: Update the privacy message for 2026: do not use personal/public accounts for identifiable data. Some institution-contracted healthcare products may support regulated workflows, but only within approved governance, contracts and access controls.
cue: Use the medication-stopping, chatbot-triage and AI-written literature review cases as boundary tests.

title: Six Exercises in 90 Minutes
summary: The lab sequence covers discharge simplification, multilingual counselling, differential diagnosis safeguards, adverse-event triage, literature review and patient-feedback analytics.
notes: Keep each exercise to 15 minutes: 3 minutes to orient, 6 minutes to run, 4 minutes to verify, and 2 minutes to record a human decision. The output is not complete until the review checklist is finished.
cue: Assign different tools to teams so the debrief compares workflows and limitations rather than merely comparing prose quality.

title: Prompt Bank and 30-60-90 Day Roadmap
summary: Reusable prompt patterns and a phased roadmap help participants move from foundation to integration and leadership while retaining data boundaries and human review.
notes: Close with one low-risk use case, one named owner, one measurable outcome, one data boundary and one stop condition. Avoid vague commitments such as 'use AI more'.
cue: Ask each team to write its first pilot as a single sentence: We will use [tool] for [task] with [data boundary], reviewed by [role], measured by [metric].
